summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Kyrgyzstan since 1998, with the age of consent set at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The constitution has banned same-sex marriage explicitly since a 2016 amendment, and no same-sex union of any kind is recognised.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. A 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision allowing trans people to change their legal gender markers, and ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that amendments to the Law on Civil Acts have left trans people unable to obtain legal recognition at all since 2021. TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 places Kyrgyzstan alongside Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia as states that removed the right to legal gender recognition, and scores Kyrgyzstan together with Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, the floor of trans legal status in their wider region.

Access to transition care has narrowed sharply. Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where previously the process could start at 18. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and from accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, and would affect minors as well as adults.

Anti-LGBT legislative pushes have been accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament, according to ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025. A 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a "positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations" through media or networks passed first reading by 79 votes to 7 in October 2014 but expired without a final vote. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law adding to Article 2-1 content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations" among information deemed harmful to children; the law does not define its key terms and does not mention sexual orientation explicitly.

No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBT people is described in the sources. ECOM data cited in the ILGA-Europe review shows high stigma and discrimination against trans people, particularly at the hands of law enforcement. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBT people on social media and dating sites, demanding payments of between 5,000 and 30,000 soms, roughly 70 to 500 US dollars. After the government launched legal reforms including an anti-gay propaganda law in 2014, attacks against LGBT people rose by nearly 300 per cent.

Organised public LGBT life in the capital has contracted. Bishkek's only gay bar, London, closed in 2017, and reporting by RFE/RL and The Guardian on the closure of the city's last LGBT club, a car-wash venue reached through a derelict yard, described patrons entering furtively as the atmosphere worsened; no other gay venue remained. In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek described as Kyrgyzstan's first gay pride march, MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks.
tangentialFactors:
TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 treats Kyrgyzstan as part of a small group of states that removed legal gender recognition, naming Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia alongside it, and rates Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at the same regional floor of merely not banning recognition.

ECOM's 2024 study on trans people's access to medical services, including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy, covers nine countries across the eastern Europe and central Asia region — Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan and Tajikistan — and includes information directed at trans migrants, placing Kyrgyzstan's care restrictions in a regional pattern of constrained transition-related healthcare.

Youth are a defined target of the informational regime. The August 2023 child protection law restricts children's access to content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations," and the 2014 anti-propaganda-style bill was framed around media accessible to minors, echoing Russia's 2013 law on propaganda to minors; the draft law of 30 January 2026 would reach minors directly through its ban on gender-affirming care.

Reporting on the closure of Bishkek's last LGBT club noted that the capital had been a relatively safe haven and liberal beacon in Central Asia until a ban on LGBT propaganda, indicating that the deterioration reached a city previously regarded as the region's most permissive.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same bars as visitors on legal gender recognition and on transition care, with the age-25 restriction in Clause 47 applying to anyone seeking care within the country rather than to travellers alone.

Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 2016 and no civil union alternative exists, so same-sex couples have no route to partner recognition, hospital access or inheritance rights through marital status.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are reported frequently, and social ostracism from friends and family is a particular concern outside the capital, in rural areas.

Police extortion of LGBT people through social media and dating platforms was documented in 2018, with demands of 5,000 to 30,000 soms, and ECOM's data indicates that law enforcement remains a primary source of stigma and discrimination against trans people.

No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBT people is described in the sources, leaving residents without a statutory complaint route in employment, housing or services.
outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch World Report 2025, Kyrgyzstan chapter, contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to terms for media repressions and freedom of expression. The placement and conditions of trans detainees therefore remain unresolved and not sourced here.

The 2020 Human Rights Watch country chapter yielded no usable finding for this record, so any change it may have documented is unresolved.

ECOM's 2024 study covers Kyrgyzstan and includes material for trans migrants, but country-level findings beyond the stigma data cited by ILGA-Europe have not been extracted, so the specific healthcare obstacles it records remain unresolved.

The status of the draft law after its first reading on 4 June 2026 is unresolved; whether it has been enacted, amended or dropped is not sourced.

Whether the August 2023 child protection amendments have been used in enforcement, and against whom, is not sourced.
